paras: The shooting of George Whittaker took place on the night of November 3, 1880, in Frankfort, Kentucky, when Frank Egbert, a young white man, shot Whittaker, a Black boy who was cheering for James A. Garfield during a Republican celebration of the presidential election. Whittaker was wounded in the side and was not expected to recover, and Egbert was later held to the Circuit Court on a $500 bond. Wire summaries bundled the shooting with the accidental wounding of a Frankfort policeman the same night under headlines about pistols and political violence in Kentucky.

On the Wednesday night after the election, Republicans in Frankfort held what the Washington Evening Star called a "jollification" and the Daily Republican a "jubilation." During the celebration a quarrel broke out between W. H. Sneed and a man named Lee, who drew a pistol; when Officer Thompson Conway intervened, the pistol went off and struck him in the abdomen. Conway died of the wound, and according to the Stanford Interior Journal he said in a dying statement that the shooting was accidental.

A few minutes after Conway was shot, Frank Egbert shot George Whittaker, who was cheering for Garfield, with the ball entering his left side just below the heart. The Daily Republican said Egbert was "incensed at a negro boy" before he drew a pistol, but no paper gave a further reason for the shooting. On November 5 the Evening Star reported that the boy was thought unlikely to recover though "somewhat easier," while a Daily Republican news summary the same day described both him and the policeman as fatally shot.

Egbert gave himself into the custody of the officers and had an examining trial before Judge Thomson. Citing the Frankfort Yeoman, the Lexington Kentucky Gazette reported that he was held for the next term of the Circuit Court in the sum of $500, which he gave. Neither Gazette brief said whether Whittaker had died, and no report of his death, recovery or of a later trial appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers mainly through brief wire items in papers outside Kentucky, which headlined it "Political Shooting in Kentucky" and "Pistols Freely Used in Kentucky" and presented the two shootings as one night's disorder. These items identified Whittaker as a "negro boy" or "colored boy" and Egbert as white, and noted that the boy was cheering for Garfield, without editorial comment. Kentucky papers gave more space to the officer's death and to Lee's paying for the funeral and deeding property to the widow than to Whittaker, whose case appeared there only in short court notes.

Accounts differed on Whittaker's condition, from "fatally" shot in one summary to not expected to recover but "somewhat easier" in another. The names in the Conway shooting also varied: Lee appeared as Jesse, Perry and Capt. Jerry Lee, Conway as Conaway, and Sneed as Snead, with the Kentucky paper giving the fullest names.

reader.title: Shooting of George Whittaker
bases: A single white man, Frank Egbert, shot a Black boy who was cheering for Garfield during a Republican celebration (A3, A4); no mob, band or officers were involved, so this is an individual political assault, while the same night's shooting of Officer Conway was a separate, reportedly accidental incident (A3, A5).
The wire reports (A2, A3, A4) and an independent Kentucky account drawn from the Frankfort Yeoman (A6) agree that Egbert shot the boy Whittaker at Frankfort on the night of Nov. 3.
